content: The brand trip is a right of passage for influencers. It’s a mark of legitimacy that a sponsor wants to invite them on an all-expenses-paid vacation, often with luxurious freebies and activities. Trips can also spur hard feelings from uninvited influencers, trigger criticism from the public, and project a certain frivolousness.  Usually it is fast fashion companies or beauty brands flying out influencers with the goal of flooding social media with sponsored content. This time, it was a major AI company. Over the weekend, several influencers began posting about OpenAI’s “first ever brand trip,” which appears to have taken place outside of New York City at a nature-filled retreat (for those curious, it looks to be the Instagram-bait Wildflower Farms). The trip was marketed as “Summer Club,” and influencers posted photos and videos from their cabins, showing off branded merch and monogrammed pajamas and talking vaguely about the scheduled programming. Many of the content creators appear to be in the career and business niches, posting about workplace culture or about being CEOs. Grace McCarrick, who has 145,000 followers on TikTok, vlogged from her suite as she ran a bath at night. Another influencer, Nat Lucy (57,000 followers), filmed herself spotting a deer outside of her cabin. All hell broke loose. [Media: https://www.tiktok.com/@graceforpersonalityhires/video/7669031978213117198] “People will literally sell their soul and their planet down the river for a nice free hotel room,” one commenter on TikTok wrote under McCarrick’s video. “Wow! Beautiful greenery! They should put a data center there!” reads a comment on Lucy’s post. Most of the videos got relatively little traction: McCarrick’s video has just under 300 likes, and Lucy’s video has fewer than 15,000 views. It’s measly engagement compared to what other splashy brand trips can command — but videos reacting to the trip have made it something of a scandal (a pair of clips alone has over half a million combined views). Many of the comments on the influencers’ videos cite the environmental effects of the AI boom, the contentious buildout of data centers across the US, and the potential for job replacement or job loss as a result of companies integrating AI in the workplace. Some also questioned why so many of the content creators who went on the trip appeared to be young women, as if OpenAI was targeting a specific demographic via media they were more connected to (though based on photos and videos posted to social media, there were men on the trip, too). According to Pew, even as the AI usage gap between men and women has all but disappeared, women tend to view AI more negatively and are twice as likely to say AI will negatively impact them personally. Some audiences wondered whether female influencers were essentially being used to launder the reputation of an industry under scrutiny.  McCarrick, who describes herself as a creator who talks about “soft skills we need at work to millions online and to teams like Spotify, Amazon, Uber and DoorDash,” has since made multiple videos responding to commenters accusing her of essentially abandoning her morals for a fancy trip. On LinkedIn she wrote that she “genuinely had no idea that people were this anti-AI,” and that the negative response to her videos exposed her to “the shocking AI psychosis running rampant online” — by which she means anger about AI, not the more common definition of being driven to paranoia or delusions of grandeur by using AI. People in the real world “do not run around like a chicken with their heads cut off, screaming about water usage and wildlife and (curiously) fascism,” she wrote. None of the influencers The Verge reached out to responded to requests for comment. OpenAI said creator marketing is part of how they reach people and that the event was meant to be educational. [Media: https://www.instagram.com/p/Dbg8k8vPKcG/] “Creators are an important part of our community and how people get information and learn about our products today,” OpenAI spokesperson Edie Campbell-Urban said in an email. “We welcome healthy debate as AI becomes more prevalent, and we value creators who choose to engage with us, attend our events, ask tough questions, and learn alongside everyone else. We’ll continue to value them, just as we do traditional media and other marketing partners.”  Setting aside the backlash to the trip for a moment, a few things stand out. First, all things considered, this appears to be a relatively simple trip. That’s not to say it wasn’t luxurious — the rooms at the retreat cost upwards of $2,000 a night — but it is nothing compared to the brands that go all out in order to milk content from every last moment (some commenters poked fun at the fact that it was a domestic trip, not a far-flung, international vacation). Second, there’s a sense that everyone involved is testing the waters: Multiple influencers noted it was the first brand trip they’d attended, and one influencer indicated they were not paid for their attendance, which big brands often do for top talent. Third and most interestingly, the goals of the trip are muddled: It’s not entirely clear what the influencers were actually doing on the trip, because there is surprisingly little content online from the event. Typically, if an influencer is on a brand trip it’s inescapable — every little luxury, every meal, every activity is TikToked and photo dumped. Instead of content about the capabilities of ChatGPT, the videos and photos are largely aspirational lifestyle content focused on the free swag and pretty setting — and even then, there’s a conspicuous lack of content, period. There isn’t the same flood of picturesque montages, clips from expert sessions or Q&As, or summaries of what a creator learned from their time with OpenAI. chineseContent: 品牌之旅是影响者的通行权。赞助商希望邀请他们参加全费用带薪假期，通常还提供豪华的免费赠品和活动，这是合法性的标志。旅行也会激起不请自来的影响者的不满，引发公众的批评，并表现出某种轻浮的态度。  通常是快时尚公司或美容品牌派出有影响力的人，目的是让社交媒体充斥赞助内容。这一次，是一家大型人工智能公司。周末，几位有影响力的人开始发布有关 OpenAI 的“第一次品牌之旅”的信息，这次旅行似乎是在纽约市郊外一个充满自然风光的度假胜地进行的（对于那些好奇的人来说，它看起来是 Instagram 上的野花农场）。这次旅行被宣传为“夏季俱乐部”，有影响力的人发布了他们小屋的照片和视频，展示了品牌商品和印有字母组合的睡衣，并含糊地谈论了预定的节目。许多内容创作者似乎都处于职业和商业领域，发布有关职场文化或首席执行官的内容。格蕾丝·麦卡里克 (Grace McCarrick) 在 TikTok 上拥有 145,000 名粉丝，她晚上在套房里一边洗澡一边发布视频博客。另一位影响者 Nat Lucy（57,000 名粉丝）拍摄了自己在小屋外发现一只鹿的视频。一切都崩溃了。 [媒体：https://www.tiktok.com/@graceforpersonalityhires/video/7669031978213117198]“人们实际上会为了一间漂亮的免费酒店房间而出卖自己的灵魂和地球，”TikTok 上的一位评论者在麦卡里克的视频下写道。 “哇！美丽的绿化！他们应该在那里建一个数据中心！”阅读对露西帖子的评论。大多数视频的吸引力相对较小：McCarrick 的视频只有不到 300 个点赞，而 Lucy 的视频只有不到 15,000 次观看
whyItMatters: 这条信息属于 AI 与科技趋势信号，适合用于观察工具选型、产品机会、开发者关注点和技术路线变化。
